content: As global mortality from acute infectious diarrhoea has declined, attention has shifted to adjunctive treatments aimed at reducing the disease burden. Smectite, a medicinal clay, has been proposed as a potential complementary therapy to shorten the duration of diarrhoea in children. To evaluate the efficacy of smectite in treating acute infectious diarrhoea in children, researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized and quasi-randomized trials. These studies compared smectite to control treatments in children aged one month to 18 years. The primary outcomes assessed were the duration of diarrhoea and clinical resolution by day 3. Data were analyzed using mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes and risk ratios (RR) for dichotomous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were performed when appropriate, and heterogeneity was assessed. Publication bias was explored using a funnel plot. Eighteen trials involving 2616 children met the inclusion criteria. These studies were conducted in both outpatient and inpatient settings, across high-income and lowor middle-income countries. Most trials included children with rotavirus infections, and approximately half involved breastfed children. The findings suggest that smectite may reduce the duration of diarrhoea by approximately 24 hours (MD -24.38 hours, 95% CI -30.91 to -17.85; 14 studies; 2209 children; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, smectite may increase the likelihood of clinical resolution by day 3 (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.30 to 3.39; 5 trials; 312 children; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce stool output (MD -11.37, 95% CI -21.94 to -0.79; 3 studies; 634 children; low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence regarding its effect on stool frequency, measured as depositions per day, is very uncertain (MD -1.33, 95% CI -2.28 to -0.38; 3 studies; 954 children; very low-certainty evidence). There was no evidence to suggest that smectite reduces the need for hospitalization (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.15; 2 studies; 885 children; low-certainty evidence) or the requirement for intravenous rehydration (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.11; 1 study; 81 children; moderate-certainty evidence). The most commonly reported side effect was constipation, but its incidence did not differ significantly between the smectite and control groups (RR 4.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 39.19; 2 studies; 128 children; low-certainty evidence). No deaths or serious adverse events were reported in the included studies. In conclusion, based on low-certainty evidence, smectite as an adjunct to rehydration therapy may reduce the duration of diarrhoea in children with acute infectious diarrhoea by approximately one day. It may also increase the likelihood of clinical resolution by day 3 and reduce stool output. However, it does not appear to affect hospitalization rates or the need for intravenous therapy.
